 On the campaign trail
 • Debate takeaways: Two GOP nominees, facing tough Senate races, put a little bit of distance between themselves and President Donald Trump during debates tonight. In Michigan, Mike Rogers acknowledged that residents were “hurting” from tens of thousands of job losses and high utility bills. In Kansas, GOP Sen. Roger Marshall mostly bear-hugged the president — with a few exceptions.
 • Red state rally: In South Carolina, Trump himself faced nearly a dozen interruptions by protesters, calling them “serious losers,” and repeated an anti-transgender slur describing Democratic candidate Annie Andrews as he campaigned for Sen. Darline Graham.
 • Ohio ad controversy: Meanwhile, Amy Acton, who is running for governor, told CNN she is “not stunned in the era we live in” by the campaign ad from her GOP opponent Vivek Ramaswamy, which features her estranged mother. Vice President JD Vance defended the campaign , saying the ad “calls it out like it is.”

 Rep. Ilhan Omar says federal agents took 17 items during search of her home
 By Piper Hudspeth Blackburn 
 Homeland Security officers carry boxes from the Washington residence of Rep. Ilhan Omar on October 12 during a search. 
 J. Scott Applewhite/AP 
 Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar said that federal agents took 17 items in the recent search of her Washington, DC, home, including several phones, notebooks and a vintage camera belonging to her husband.
 “It was very bizarre,” she told MS NOW in an interview that aired Wednesday, describing the hourslong search that took place earlier this month.
 Omar recalled waking up around 6 a.m. the morning of October 12, hearing pounding on both the front and back door of her home. “I thought something was on fire. I thought something was happening to the neighbors. Like it sounded like an urgent evacuation sort of situation,” she said.
 CNN previously reported that the search was related to an immigration fraud probe investigating whether Omar’s father lied about her age when she obtained her US citizenship in 2000. Omar has sought to dismantle the basis of the probe, saying she became a lawfully naturalized citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia in 1995.
 “I take it very seriously, and I’m sure my lawyers are taking it very seriously,” she told MS NOW.

 Trump continues using anti-transgender slur to attack Democrat Annie Andrews
 By Kit Maher 
 US President Donald Trump leaves after speaking at a campaign rally at T. Ed Garrison Arena in Pendleton, South Carolina on October 21. 
 Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump again used an anti-transgender slur to describe South Carolina Senate nominee and pediatrician Annie Andrews, calling her “Trannie Annie” while campaigning for Republican challenger Darline Graham .
 “Darline’s running against a radical left lunatic named ‘Trannie’ Annie Andrews,” Trump said in South Carolina Wednesday night. He referred to her by the slur twice tonight and called her a “fanatical transgender activist.”
 “She claims to be a moderate. But she’s really a rabid advocate for taxpayer-funded child sexual mutilation,” Trump said. “That’s where she is, and she’s never going to change.”
 Earlier this month – a few days after Trump first called her the slur – Andrews released a direct-to-camera ad clarifying her stance on transgender issues.
 “I want you to hear me loud and clear: I don’t support biological men playing women’s sports and I don’t support – and haven’t ever performed – gender surgery for minors,” she said.
 Trump earlier this week used an antisemitic term during his remarks in Kansas.

 Kansas GOP Sen. Roger Marshall mostly bear-hugs Trump — with a couple exceptions
 By Aaron Blake 
 President Donald Trump and Republican US Senate reelection candidate Roger Marshall greet each other during a rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday. 
 Jonathan Ernst/Reuters 
 Kansas GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in Wednesday’s debate mostly bear-hugged President Donald Trump and his agenda — with a few exceptions. When asked about Trump being unpopular even in red Kansas, Marshall turned it into an appeal to Trump supporters.
 “I’ve had multiple times when I’ve objected to the president before, but I do want to emphasize: We need the Trump voters to come out,” Marshall said. “And that would be my appeal tonight to people: If you want the Trump agenda to continue, if you want secure borders, if you want a strong military, if you want lower taxes … you need to come out, because we delivered on those things.”
 Marshall also embraced Trump’s tariffs, which he credited for revitalizing manufacturing in Kansas.
 But when pressed on where he differs with Trump, he cited some of ICE’s tactics and Trump’s move to import beef.
 “The first thing I did when I saw what was going on in Southwest Kansas [with ICE raids], I picked up the phone, called [Homeland Security] Secretary Markwayne Mullin and said, ‘Hey, I don’t think this is quite right. What’s going on?” Marshall said.

 Kansas hopefuls respond to biggest attack lines against them
 Analysis by Aaron Blake 
 Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, right, and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Adam Hamilton participate in a debate at WDAF TV in Kansas City, Missouri, on October 21. 
 Charlie Riedel/Pool/AP 
 At the start of Wednesday’s Senate debate in Kansas, both GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton were asked about some of the biggest subjects of their opponent’s attack ads.
 For Marshall, that’s his having sued hundreds of patients over unpaid medical bills as a doctor, according to a New York Times investigation last month. Marshall was asked if he ever intervened to stop his office from sending one of the cases to collection.
 “I think there were times when the collection people would come to me and say, ‘Hey, we think you should do something on this one,’” Marshall said. “But we already wrote off many, many bills as well. Generally speaking, once it was turned over to collections, it was done.”
 Hamilton was pressed on his handling of alleged child sex abuse allegations against a volunteer at a church camp two decades ago, when the initial accusations weren’t immediately reported to police.
 Hamilton said the policy was wrong and was later changed to share the information with police. He emphasized the later police investigation was inconclusive but said he should have prevented the man from returning to the camp the next year.
 “I did not sign off on him going back,” Hamilton said. “I should have checked to make sure that he wasn’t going back. That was a mistake on my part.”

 Rogers makes direct appeal to supporters of losing candidate in Democratic primary
 By Gloria Pazmino 
 As he continued to cast Abdul El-Sayed as too extreme, Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers made a direct appeal to supporters of Rep. Haley Stevens, who El-Sayed defeated in the Democratic primary.
 “You’re a Haley Stevens voter, and you came out of this and you said, ‘Man, I just can’t do it. He’s too extreme,’” Rogers said. “Well guess what, you have a home with us.”
 He also sought to appeal to Jewish Democrats, a group that El-Sayed has struggled to win over after the primary amid his staunch criticism of Israel’s government.
 Rogers spent much of the debate trying to tie El-Sayed to the Democratic Socialists of America and suggesting his progressive policies would exacerbate issues of affordability.
 “It really isn’t about left versus right anymore. It really is about the heart and soul of the country and who we are as Americans and the future we want for our children,” Rogers said.

 El-Sayed says Rogers' Muslim Brotherhood allegations are "shameful"
 By Gloria Pazmino 
 Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed ripped into his Republican opponent Mike Rogers as he continued to suggest he has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.
 In a tense exchange, El-Sayed said Rogers should be ashamed as a former member of Congress who had sworn an oath to defend the Constitution.
 “It’s really quite beneath you to call into question my loyalty to the Constitution,” El-Sayed said. “It is actually really quite shameful.”
 In turn, Rogers accused El-Sayed of trying to play “the victim.”
 The Islamist political movement has become a flashpoint in Michigan’s Senate race, with Republicans zeroing in on old tweets from his half-sister, including a post from 2012 in which she described having “an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college.”
 El-Sayed, who could make history as the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, has denounced the group and said he is unaware of anyone in his family having ties to it.
 “He keeps raising this question about this association with an organization I’ve never been a part of, because my mom was a nurse in Missouri, it doesn’t make any sense,” El-Sayed said. “It’s actually really quite beneath you, Mike, it’s really quite beneath you.”

 New Fox News poll on Senate races shows Democratic edge in Ohio and tight race in Texas
 By Jennifer Agiesta 
 Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown leads Republican Sen. Jon Husted in the critical Senate race in Ohio, while there is no clear leader in the Senate race in Texas between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton, according to new polling from Fox News and CNN’s Poll of Polls averages on these races.
 According to the average, Brown leads Husted 49% to 44% across recent high-quality polling of likely voters in Ohio. Brown held a lead outside of the margin of error in 4 of the 5 included surveys on the race.
 In Texas, Talarico averages 49% support to Paxton’s 47% in high-quality polling. Polling on that race largely shows no clear leader.
 The new Fox News poll finds a tied contest there.
 In Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton holds an edge over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in the fiercely contested gubernatorial race, according to the CNN Poll of Polls; Acton averages 50% support to Ramaswamy’s 44%. All polls included in the current average were completed before news about an ad f eaturing Acton’s estranged mother became public.

 Trump calls protesters interrupting rally in South Carolina "serious losers"
 By Kit Maher and Alayna Treene 
 A protester shouts as US President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally at T. Ed Garrison Arena in Pendleton, South Carolina on October 21. 
 Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump’s rally in South Carolina has been interrupted by at least 11 protesters, so far, who have yelled out opposition to the president at different times during his remarks, one within just a few minutes of him taking the podium.
 “I don’t mind when they do that, but it’s always right at my punchline … I’ve had three punchlines, and three of them, they time them beautifully. They time them beautifully. These people are serious losers,” Trump said.
 Several screamed “f**k you!” at Trump. Some called him a “traitor.”
 “These people are crazy,” Trump said. He also appeared to admire a person who threw a punch, before law enforcement dragged another protester out of the event.
 “I watched that. I saw that. That was incredible. Wow, that was unbelievable. Is everybody okay?” Trump said. “Who is the guy that threw that punch?”
 Trump is campaigning for Darline Graham, who is running for her late brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat. The president said her opponent, pediatrician Annie Andrews, “would be the most extreme and crazy left-wing politician ever elected in this state.”

 On Iran war, El-Sayed and Rogers exchange jabs on Trump and Muslim Brotherhood
 By Gloria Pazmino 
 Republican Candidate for United States Senator Mike Rogers and Democratic Candidate for United States Senator Abdul El-Sayed debate in Michigan on October 21, 2026. 
 WXYZ/Scripps 
 Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said his opponent Mike Rogers and President Donald Trump are “hip to hip” on the Iran war during tonight’s debate.
 “If you don’t believe me, I want you to pay attention on Sunday when Donald Trump comes here at the invitation of Mike Rogers to remind you that, in fact, Donald Trump is on the ballot through Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said.
 The remarks came after El-Sayed was asked whether he believed Iran poses a significant threat to US national security and what the country’s strategy should be on the matter. The Democrat did not directly answer the question, saying Iran “had posed” a threat in the past, crediting former President Barack Obama for using diplomacy to contain it during his administration, before criticizing Trump’s decision to launch a war with the country.
 Rogers, however, said Iran is “absolutely” a threat to the United States but declined to say how he thought the country should handle it.
 Notably, the former congressman had initially voiced support for the war in Iran, but he has since called for an end for the conflict.
 He then used the conflict in Iran to again suggest El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, a group the Democrat has disavowed , and questioned his loyalty to the United States.
 “So being bought off by the Muslim Brotherhood, having donors to his campaign from Hamas that support Hezbollah, is not a problem,” Rogers said. “If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?”

 Rogers and El-Sayed trade barbs: "Pattern of deception" vs. "MAGA bingo"
 By Stephen Collinson 
 Republican Mike Rogers’ top debate task tonight is to disqualify Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the minds of undecided Michigan voters.
 He’s therefore arguing that his opponent cannot by trusted — and sympathizes with Islamic extremists and is a Democratic Socialist in disguise.
 “There is, again that whole pattern of deception,” Rogers said of El-Sayed’s claim to be in favor of strong border enforcement, using a refrain to which he frequently returned.
 Pushing back on El-Sayed’s denials that he wants to defund the police, Rogers claimed “this guy has got new, false information about every 30 seconds.”
 El-Sayed countered multiple times that it was Rogers who was being untruthful and said he was playing a classic game of distraction practiced by President Donald Trump.
 His repeated refrain was that viewers should be playing “MAGA bingo” at home as they tick off Rogers pre-planned attacks.
 “That is the debate and the Michigan campaign in a nutshell. Rogers must paint his rival as an unacceptable choice. El-Sayed is arguing that Rogers equals Trump.

 Democratic candidate for governor of Ohio, Amy Acton, received support at a campaign event in Wharton, Ohio, over the incendiary attack ad from her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy.
 “My heart goes out to you,” one supporter told Acton. “Can I give you a hug?”
 After the two shared a hug, Acton then spoke to the room of supporters about her and her brother’s relationship with their estranged mother, which was the subject of the political ad.
 “We experienced a lot of neglect and abuse,” she continued. “The reason I talk about my childhood, and when I do, is just … I started to realize it might give other people hope that you can get out of circumstances.”

 Rogers breaks with Trump's economic vision at top of debate
 By Stephen Collinson 
 Unlike the president, who is proclaiming an economic “golden age,” GOP ex-Rep. Mike Rogers admitted near the start of the Senate race debate that Michiganders were “hurting” from tens of thousands of lost jobs and the highest utilities bills in the Midwest.
 He walked a fine line on tariffs, arguing that some were working to bring jobs home from Mexico and China, but that the trade war with Canada — a huge issue in Michigan’s border state economy — was not well thought through. Rogers argued that Democratic control of Congress would cause higher taxes and higher costs, including for gasoline.
 Democrat Abdul El-Sayed had an easier task given huge public dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy — and claimed the president and Rogers stood “hip to hip.” He said voters should send him to the Senate to ensure “money is going to be spent on you and your kids, rather than dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids.”

 Mike Rogers immediately tries to tie Abdul El-Sayed to DSA as final debate gets underway
 By Gloria Pazmino 
 In his opening statement, Republican US Senate nominee Mike Rogers sought to cast his opponent, Democratic nominee Adbul El-Sayed as “aligned” with the Democratic Socialists of America.
 El-Sayed is not a member of the DSA, but he is allied and supported by several members of the group, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez who campaigned with him through Michigan’s Upper Peninsula last week.
 El-Sayed also supports policies backed by the DSA, such as Medicare for All but he has previously described himself as a “capitalist.”

 Some South Carolina Republicans see alternative to Darline Graham: "Write In Ralph”
 By Dianne Gallagher 
 Rep. Ralph Norman speaks during a markup meeting with the House Budget Committee on Capitol Hill in September 2023. 
 Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images/FILE 
 Sen. Darline Graham has been working to unite her party since winning a particularly bruising Republican special primary and runoff election this summer.
 But the lingering discontent has led some supporters of losing GOP candidates to start the “Write-In Ralph” campaign, encouraging Republican voters to write in her runoff opponent Rep. Ralph Norman’s name, instead of voting for Graham in the general election.
 Norman is not affiliated with the group, has endorsed Graham and says he supports the Republican ticket. But the congressman said in a podcast interview released today that his family would not vote for Graham in November.
 “I’m going to do what I said personally,” Norman said on “the Nashional Briefing with Kelly Nash.” “My family is not going to vote for Darline Graham. They’re just not. Now they’re grown and with their own children can do what they want. But I will because I promised to do that.”
 One of the founders of the write-in movement, Avery Milton, told CNN this month that the campaign started in part because the heavy national influence on the special primary, especially from President Donald Trump, felt “fundamentally unfair.”
 Political experts in the state don’t think the effort has any real teeth, but it has received attention on social media – especially as Democrat Annie Andrews has been gaining ground in the typically reliably Republican state.
 Milton says since the race is competitive some Republicans have complained that their campaign could help a Democrat win the Senate seat for the first time since 1998.
 “It would be a loss, but we see it as a loss either way. There’s really no winning here for us, as grassroots conservatives,” said Milton. “It could be a lot easier to deal with a one-term Democrat senator than another 20 years of a ‘Graham-nsty.’”

 “I’m not stunned in the era we live in,” Acton told CNN about the ad, which has spurred controversy.

 Ohio Democratic lawmaker gets emotional when asked about the controversial Ramaswamy ad

 Trump, who said he gave Putin nothing, ties sanction waivers to release of freed American
 By Kit Maher 
 US special envoy Steve Witkoff, center, speaks with Stephen Hubbard, right, in Saint Petersburg, Russia, on Wednesday. 
 Reuters 
 President Donald Trump directly tied the waiving of Russia-related sanctions to the release of an American detained in Russia , despite stating earlier that the United States gave Moscow “nothing in exchange” for the freed American.
 “If you were to put those sanctions on, or whatever you want to call them, you could forget about him,” Trump told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, referring to Stephen Hubbard, who had been imprisoned in Russia for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
 “You’d never see him again,” Trump added, arguing that easing sanctions was part of smoothing over negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
 Earlier Wednesday in the East Room, however, Trump said, “We gave nothing in exchange, which is very rare.”
 The measures Trump most recently waived were part of legislation named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed earlier this year. Some Republicans — including the late senator’s sister, Sen. Darline Graham, for whom Trump is campaigning Wednesday night — have expressed their disagreement with the president’s move.
 When Collins asked Trump what Graham said to him about the sanctions, the president immediately pivoted to talking about the freed American.
 “We were in the midst of negotiating (Hubbard’s release), and a lot of stupid people said, and people that don’t know how life works, they said, ‘Why aren’t you putting Russia sanctions,’ and all this, in the midst of a negotiation to try and get a long-term hostage back from Russia.”
 Trump posted on Truth Social earlier Wednesday that “Numerous people, who requested that sanctions be immediately imposed on Russia, have called to apologize to President Trump in that they didn’t know that he was negotiating the release of Stephen Hubbard.”

 President Donald Trump is heading to Mississippi for a rally next week, the latest evidence that Republicans are scrambling to shore up their base in the midterms.
 Trump won Mississippi by double digits in all three of his presidential campaigns, including by 23 percentage points in 2024. But the Senate race there has become increasingly competitive, with national Democrats starting to spend in the contest.
 Trump’s rally will be Monday in Corinth, a small city in the northeastern corner of the state, according to the Republican National Committee. It’s his latest stop in a red state as Republicans try to rally their core voters to turn out in a difficult national environment.
 In Mississippi, GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is looking to overcome Democrat Scott Colom, a local district attorney, in her reelection bid. Senate Majority PAC, the top Democratic super PAC in Senate elections, announced Tuesday it would begin spending in the state, launching a $1.2 million ad campaign through Election Day.

 Trump calls Iran war "one of the greatest things we've done"
 By Betsy Klein 
 President Donald Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Wednesday. 
 Alex Brandon/AP 
 President Donald Trump on Wednesday called the US war against Iran “one of the greatest things we’ve done,” despite the conflict remaining deeply unpopular at home and many GOP candidates calling for it to end.
 Asked Wednesday if he regrets starting the war, Trump told reporters, “No, I think it’s one of the greatest things — I think it’s one of the greatest things we’ve done.”
 “We’ve stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon. It’s one of the best things that we’ve done,” he continued, going on to say that his decision to attack Iran in February “took a lot of courage.”
 But nearly eight months since the start of the war, the president is getting low marks: a new CNN poll out Wednesday showed that just 30% of Americans approve of his handling of foreign affairs. CNN has spoken with many voters, including at the president’s rallies, who have pointed to the conflict’s impact on gas prices and the cost of living as a major issue in the upcoming election.
 Meanwhile, some Republicans facing tough elections this fall have been distancing themselves from the president on the war.
